title: What each side means by affirming or denying freedom before grace
source_text: LVII. Nam dum negant Protestantes hominem ante gratiam libertatem suam habere, quantum spectat ad opera spiritualia & supernaturalia, per id negare non intendunt hominem ante gratiam praeditum esse ea libertate, quae voluntati essentialis est, & quae opponitur necessitati Physicae & brutae determinationi, etiam circa res spirituales & supernaturales: adeoque hominem in eo statu libere omittere actus supernaturales in Evangelio praeceptos; quum vero per gratiam movetur, iisdem actibus libere defungi, & sic aut aliter agendi, saltem in sensu diviso, veram potestatem habeat: sed illud solum sibi volunt hominem in eo statu non esse liberum a servitute peccati, & a dependentia motionis divinae per auxilium supernaturale, & sine tali auxilio, in negotio salutis eum nihil omnino posse. Quum vero Schola Romana affirmat hominem ante gratiam liberum esse in rebus spiritualibus & quae ad pietatem spectant, per id inficiari non vult hominem ante gratiam esse peccati servum, & nihil prorsus eum sine gratia posse, in iis in quibus vera erga Deum pietas consistit. Sed mens ejus solum est, hominem per naturam talem esse, & ea essentiali libertate praeditum, ut gratia auxiliante libere in bonum feratur, & veram semper potestatem habeat illud faciendi, aut non faciendi.
pass_a_gloss: LVII. For while the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom, as far as regards spiritual and supernatural works, by that they do not intend to deny that man before grace is endowed with that freedom, which is essential to the will, and which is opposed to Physical necessity and brute determination, even about spiritual and supernatural things: and so that man in that state freely omits the supernatural acts prescribed in the Gospel; but when he is moved through grace, freely performs the same acts, and has a true power of acting so or otherwise, at least in the divided sense: but they mean only this, that man in that state is not free from the servitude of sin, and from dependence on the divine motion through supernatural help, and that without such help, in the business of salvation he can do nothing at all. But when the Roman School affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and those which regard piety, by that it does not wish to deny that man before grace is the slave of sin, and that he can do nothing at all without grace, in those things in which true piety toward God consists. But its mind only is, that man is by nature such, and endowed with that essential freedom, that, grace helping, he is freely borne to good, and always has a true power of doing it, or of not doing it.
pass_b_english: When the Protestants deny that man before grace has his freedom with respect to spiritual and supernatural works, they do not mean to deny that man before grace has the freedom essential to the will, opposed to physical necessity and brute determination, even regarding spiritual and supernatural things.

So they allow that man in that state leaves undone freely the supernatural acts the Gospel commands; and that when grace moves him he performs those acts freely and has a real power to act one way or the other, at least in the divided sense. All they mean is that man in that state is not free from bondage to sin or from dependence on God's motion through supernatural help, and that without such help he can do nothing whatever in the matter of salvation.

When the Roman School, for its part, affirms that man before grace is free in spiritual things and things of piety, it does not mean to deny that man before grace is a slave of sin and can do nothing at all without grace in the things that make up true piety toward God. It means only that man is by nature so made, and so endowed with that essential freedom, that with grace helping he moves freely toward good and always has a real power to do it or not do it.
